lesson.title: Reading the Rainbow: The Resistor Color Code
lesson.summary: The resistor color code encodes a resistor's value and tolerance in painted bands, with digit colors, a multiplier band, and a tolerance band that together replace printed text on a component too small to label.
lesson.body:
Every resistor is built to a nominal value, but printing that number in tiny text on a component a few millimeters long is impractical and easy to smudge into unreadability, so the industry settled on a color band code instead: a sequence of painted rings around the resistor body that encodes the value and its tolerance in a format readable from any angle and immune to fading text. Learning to read it is a purely practical skill, but it rests directly on understanding what a resistor is and why its value matters in every calculation this chapter has relied on so far.

The standard four band code assigns each color a digit from 0 to 9: black is 0, brown is 1, red is 2, orange is 3, yellow is 4, green is 5, blue is 6, violet is 7, gray is 8, and white is 9. The first two bands give the two significant digits of the value. The third band is a multiplier, the same color scale but read as a power of ten to multiply by, so red as a multiplier means times 100, orange means times 1000, and so on. The fourth band gives the tolerance, how far the actual resistance may legitimately differ from the printed value: gold means plus or minus 5 percent, silver means plus or minus 10 percent, and brown means plus or minus 1 percent.

Reading an example: a resistor with bands brown, black, red, gold. Brown gives the first digit, 1. Black gives the second digit, 0. Together that is 10. Red as the third band means multiply by 100, giving 10 times 100, or 1000 ohms, which is 1 kilohm. Gold as the fourth band means the tolerance is plus or minus 5 percent. Five percent of 1000 ohms is 50 ohms, so the actual resistance is guaranteed to fall somewhere between 950 ohms and 1050 ohms, even though only 1000 ohms is printed on the part.

Higher precision resistors often use a five band code instead: the first three bands are significant digits, the fourth band is the multiplier, and the fifth is tolerance. For example, red, red, black, brown, brown reads as digits 2, 2, 0, giving 220, then brown as the multiplier means times 10, giving 220 times 10, or 2200 ohms, and the final brown band means plus or minus 1 percent tolerance. One percent of 2200 ohms is 22 ohms, so the true value lies between 2178 ohms and 2222 ohms.

Recognizing these bands quickly is a workshop skill, not a derived law, but it matters for exactly the same reason every calculation in this chapter matters: every KVL equation, every node voltage, every mesh current computed by hand assumes the resistor values plugged in are correct, and a resistor pulled from a mixed parts bin is only as trustworthy as your ability to read its bands correctly before it goes anywhere near a breadboard. One practical habit worth building is to always read the bands starting from the end closest to one edge of the resistor body, since the tolerance band is typically spaced slightly farther from its neighbors than the digit bands are from each other, and when a color could plausibly be read from either direction, a multimeter measurement across the leads is the fastest way to confirm which reading is correct before it gets soldered into a circuit.
